abstract: Normothermic machine perfusion (NMP) is used to preserve and assess donor livers, but current viability criteria rely on global measures that do not resolve intracellular metabolism, which would provide a more mechanistic measure of donor liver function. We combined staged ex vivo perfusion of mouse livers, serial lobectomy and 13C tracers ([U-13C3]lactate, [U-13C3]pyruvate and [U-13C6]glucose) to test whether glucose fragment-based flux models used in vivo describe intact hepatic metabolism. With intracellular metabolite isotopomers as constraints, a homogeneous one-compartment model failed to fit most datasets, and the lack of fit centered on TCA cycle intermediates such as malate. A two-compartment model, in which a glycolytic compartment takes up glucose from the sinusoidal pool, including glucose released by a gluconeogenic compartment, fitted 41 of 45 datasets. Flux partitioning between compartments depended on nutritional state, which influenced hepatic metabolism more than perfusate glucose. Nevertheless, glucose fragment and two-compartment flux estimates correlated (R2 = 0.68-0.89). Intracellular isotope tracing thus shows that hepatic compartmentation constrains whole-liver flux estimation, while supporting simplified models for quantitative assessment during perfusion.
